attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Going to happen a lot' is a firm, undated forecast. Its referent is the sly opt-out playbook named in the preceding sentence. 'Be on your guard' is advice and is not graded.

contract.note: Reading 'a lot' as a recurrent practice across companies, with concealed defaults, is an ordinary plain reading. It invents no count and does not treat a lack of examples as failure.

evidence.note: A policy-monitor memo dated Jan 2026 shows that Starlink added AI training with an opt-out. It is one company and does not show concealment, so it cannot establish a widespread pattern.
Anthropic's own announcement (Aug 2025) of a training choice shown in a pop-up. It is a company disclosure. It shows not every policy change is covert, but it does not rule out the forecast.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The packet has one possible example (Starlink) and one prominently disclosed counterexample (Anthropic). Nothing systematic shows a broad, repeated pattern of hidden opt-out training. The early-resolution rule is not met and nothing decisive rules the forecast out.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'We can expect more companies' is unqualified expectation, so it is a scored forecast. The proposition keeps both parts: the opt-out default and the hiding in obscure settings or terms.

contract.note: Requiring at least two more companies is a fair minimum for 'more companies'. Requiring concealment follows the speaker's own word 'hiding'. Reading 'nobody reads' as rhetoric is reasonable.

evidence.note: Reuters, Jan 2026: Starlink added AI training unless users opt out, and its scope is unclear. Nothing shows how affected users were notified, so the concealment part is not established.
Vercel's own changelog, Mar 2026: Hobby and trial users are opted in by default, and the change was announced publicly in advance. That cuts against treating it as concealed.
A secondary blog, Mar 2025, reports that Pinterest opted users in by default but notified them in advance. It is an uncertain example of concealment.

reviews.rationale: Several companies adopted opt-out training defaults after the post. But the packet does not show two complete cases where notice was confined to obscure settings or terms: Vercel and Pinterest gave advance notice, and Starlink's notices are unknown. The forecast has no deadline and nothing decisive contradicts it, so it stays open.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He relays a LinkedIn post but adopts the point, with hedges, in his own statement.

semantics.note: An observation about current practice, qualified by 'apparently' and 'maybe most'. These are evidential and probabilistic hedges, not a firm commitment that the practice is happening.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading and scores the claim even though it notes the 'apparently' hedge. Under policy, plain-reading scoring applies only to firm language. It also narrows 'scraping' to training large language models, which the speaker did not specify.

evidence.note: Microsoft's denial dated Nov 25, 2024, in the target period: it says it does not train large language models on Microsoft 365 data. This is a company statement about itself, not an independent audit.

The Register, Nov 27, 2024: connected features analyse document content, but training is not established. The report repeats Microsoft's denial and notes an unanswered question about what 'permission' means.

reviews.rationale: The statement is hedged: Microsoft is 'apparently' scraping, 'maybe most' subscribers. Under policy, hedged claims are not scored. For reference only: the evidence is mainly Microsoft's own denial that it trains large language models on this data, and no independent audit is available.
